west-bank-substation-land-taking-eump.title: Land taken from 38 owners for four West Bank power substations, with compensation unfinished when the works began
west-bank-substation-land-taking-eump.place: Sarra village, Nablus Governorate, with almqeblih near Jenin, Beit Oula near Hebron and Qalandia near Ramallah, West Bank, Palestine
west-bank-substation-land-taking-eump.point: Sarra village in Nablus Governorate, the site of one of the four substations. Coordinates from OpenStreetMap's Nominatim search for Sarra. The land was taken at four separate sites, so this point stands for one of them.

lenders.name: World Bank
lenders.role: Electric Utility Management Project, project number P084461, financed by two trust fund grants, TF-92336 and TF-94587. The original commitment was US$12.0 million and US$14.5 million was disbursed; the grant agreement for TF092336 is dated 30 June 2008 (Implementation Completion and Results Report, ICR00002455, 24 March 2017, data sheet and Annex 10). The Bank approved the project on 15 May 2008 and it closed on 30 September 2016, three years after the original closing date of 30 September 2013. The project was environmental Category B. The appraisal document's safeguard table marks two policies and only two: Environmental Assessment (OP/BP 4.01) and Involuntary Resettlement (OP/BP 4.12), with Natural Habitats, Pest Management, Physical Cultural Resources, Indigenous Peoples, Forests, Safety of Dams, Projects in Disputed Areas and Projects on International Waterways all marked no (Project Appraisal Document, report no. 43298-62, 22 April 2008, section III.F). In September 2013 a Bank supervision mission found the Palestinian Energy and Natural Resources Authority non-compliant with Bank safeguard policies at three of the four substations, Jenin, Nablus and Hebron, because civil works had started before the Bank cleared and disclosed the environmental and resettlement instruments; the safeguards rating was upgraded to Moderately Satisfactory from Unsatisfactory in May 2014 and kept until closing (completion report, paragraph 30). The completion report rates the project's overall outcome Moderately Satisfactory. The Bank's Independent Evaluation Group rates the outcome Moderately Unsatisfactory, on a split rating weighted by the 81 per cent of trust fund financing disbursed at restructuring, and rates risk to development outcome High (ICR Review, ICRR0020707, 2017, sections 6, 7 and 11a).

lenders.name: European Investment Bank
lenders.role: Financed the four 161/33/22 kV substations, which were Component 1 of the project the Bank appraised and the component the land was taken for. The completion report records an original EIB loan of EUR 45 million effective in 2005, restructured during implementation, and EIB internal approval of a EUR 44.5 million single-source contract for the construction of the four substations by the Israel Electric Corporation, signed in February 2012. The component's actual cost is given as US$56.5 million, mostly EIB with Norwegian funding for some auxiliary equipment (completion report, paragraphs 13 and 25, and the donor contributions table). The World Bank's own grants paid for other components: the central distribution system, distribution rehabilitation, capacity building, consultancies and the start-up costs of the new transmission company and regulator.

companies.name: Palestinian Energy and Natural Resources Authority
companies.role: Implementing agency, the Palestinian Authority body responsible for the energy sector; its Project Management Unit ran the project. Its Land Acquisition Committee assessed the price of each parcel and a Land Evaluation Committee valued the land against neighbouring parcel prices; the expropriation decrees required cabinet approval and confirmation by the office of the president. This is the body the Bank's September 2013 mission found non-compliant with its safeguard policies at three of the four substations (completion report, paragraph 30; Resettlement Action Plan, March 2011, sections 2.2 and 2.3).

companies.name: Israel Electric Corporation
companies.role: Built the four substations under a single-source contract approved by the European Investment Bank. The completion report says the Palestinian Authority and EIB concluded that only this company could effectively build the substations in the West Bank, because of the complexity of the approval processes from the Israeli authorities and the need to deal with them, and that it took from May 2008 to October 2010 to agree contract terms, partly because the company had no obvious interest in speeding up construction, which would cut its short-term electricity sales to the West Bank (completion report, paragraph 25).

west-bank-substation-land-taking-eump.community: Four high-voltage substations needed land at four sites. The project's Resettlement Action Plan of March 2011 names them and counts the people whose land was taken. At Jenin, 15,028 square metres were taken from 23 owners, including, in the plan's spelling, owners of almqeblih village; the plan says that process 'has already been conducted by Palestinian industrial Zone', that the ownership of the 15,028 square metres 'is transferred to PEA', and that JD 66,315.20, assessed at JD 4.41 per square metre, 'has to be paid for the 23 owner'. So the Jenin land was taken through the industrial zone and transferred on, not acquired by the energy authority itself. At Sarra village in Nablus Governorate, 15,174 square metres belonging to 10 owners, with JD 349,000 assessed at JD 23 per square metre to be paid. At Beit Oula village near Hebron, about 17,524 square metres from 4 owners, with JD 89,898 assessed at JD 5.13 per square metre to be paid. At Qalandia, 11,000 square metres bought directly, with one person listed as affected and no price yet set. The plan's summary table lists the four sites with 23, 10, 4 and 1 persons affected. It records the status of each: the Jenin process 'finish', Sarra and Beit Oula awaiting cabinet approval, Qalandia still at the estimation stage. The plan's two accounts of the Jenin site do not agree. Its summary table marks the Jenin status 'Resettlement process finish', while its annexed compensation table for the same three parcels gives 23 owners, JD 66,315.2 awarded, no expropriation decree number, no expropriation date, and in the comments column: 'Assessed amount not yet awarded'. That annex also names each owner, with the parcel, the land title number, the area in dunams and a column for the owner's national identity card number: 23 people at Jenin across parcels 8/1, 10/1 and 11/1, in Almqebleh title 20010 and Berqin title 2, plus a 0.468-dunam road strip. The plan also sets out when people were to be consulted: Qalandia in September 2011 and Jenin, Nablus and Hebron in June 2012, after the assessments had been made. For Sarra and Beit Oula the plan says notices with the owners' names and land titles were published twice in local newspapers and that no owner objected. The plan says the land was taken by expropriation under the 1953 Land Acquisition Law, applied in the West Bank from Jordanian legislation, and that it remains hard to seek remedies in the Palestinian court system because of uncertainty over enforcement and the limits of a court system operating under occupation. The project's completion report of 24 March 2017 records what happened next: at Jenin, Nablus and Hebron, civil works began before the Bank had cleared and disclosed the resettlement and environmental instruments, and 'project affected people were identified prior to construction and the compensation process had started but it had not yet been completed'. The same paragraph says the issue was solved thanks to the proactivity of the Bank team and for the benefit of EIB, and that the safeguards rating was upgraded in May 2014. A footnote to that paragraph records that the Bank's Jerusalem office received a complaint by email from the closest neighbour to the Nablus substation; the task team met the complainant, four other neighbours and the mayor, raised their concerns with the Palestinian authority and EIB, and sent the complainant a written response. The footnote does not say what the complaint was about. No document found counts anyone moved out of a home.
west-bank-substation-land-taking-eump.displaced_note: ICIJ gives 38 for this project, which is its count of project-affected people and not a count of people moved. The Resettlement Action Plan of March 2011 lists 38 persons affected across the four substation sites, in a table whose column is headed 'Number of person affected': 23 at Jenin, 10 at Sarra, 4 at Beit Oula and 1 at Qalandia. No document found counts anyone relocated, and the plan describes the parcels as land rather than housing.
west-bank-substation-land-taking-eump.outcome: The project closed on 30 September 2016. Three of the four substations were complete at closing; the fourth, at Ramallah, was 15 per cent complete, held up by permits from the Israeli authorities for works in Area C, and was planned for commissioning in July 2018. The two reports do not agree on where the compensation ended up. The completion report says the compensation process had started but had not yet been completed when the works began, and that the issue was solved. The Independent Evaluation Group's review reads the same page as meaning that 'although project affected people were identified prior to the commencement of construction activities, the compensation process had not been completed by project closure', adds that the task team leader subsequently informed the Group that the process was later completed, and says the completion report does not state whether the compensation and resettlement processes conformed to the requirements of OP 4.12. The statement that the process was completed is attributed to Bank staff, not to any document.

west-bank-substation-land-taking-eump.confidence_note: Every figure here comes from the lender's own papers: the Bank's completion report, the Bank's appraisal document, the Bank's Independent Evaluation Group and a resettlement plan written by the borrower's own energy authority for the Bank. No independent press report, court record, audit or panel finding about the land taken at these four sites was found. Two further limits. The compensation amounts are sums assessed; the plan's annex for Jenin says the assessed amount was not yet awarded while its summary table calls that site's process finished, and no document says any owner was paid in full or that any named owner went permanently uncompensated. And the substations the land was taken for were financed by the European Investment Bank, not by the Bank's grants, although they were Component 1 of the project the Bank appraised, were covered by the resettlement policy framework the Bank required, and were supervised and rated by the Bank for safeguard compliance.

ahwaz-jomhori-pumping-station-house-expr.title: House on Jomhori Boulevard expropriated for an Ahwaz sewerage pumping station
ahwaz-jomhori-pumping-station-house-expr.place: Jomhori Boulevard, Ahwaz, Khuzestan Province, Iran
ahwaz-jomhori-pumping-station-house-expr.point: Ahwaz city. The completion report names only Jomhori Boulevard, which OpenStreetMap's Nominatim search does not return, so the point is the city centre from Nominatim's result for Ahvaz.

lenders.name: World Bank (IBRD)
lenders.role: Ahwaz and Shiraz Water Supply and Sanitation Project, project number P071191, Loan 4738-IR. The loan agreement of 17 July 2004 lends US$279,000,000 to the Islamic Republic of Iran (Loan Agreement, Section 2.01). The Board approved it on 25 May 2004, it became effective on 17 November 2004 and it closed on 30 September 2009 without extension; US$200.6 million was disbursed (Implementation Completion and Results Report, ICR00001441, 31 March 2010, data sheet). The project was environmental Category A, because of the water and wastewater treatment plants, sludge and effluent reuse, industrial effluent discharge and the archaeological sites in Shiraz; the completion report says OP 4.01 on Environmental Assessment was triggered, that OPN 11.03 on cultural property was also triggered for Shiraz, and that the project received an exemption from OP 7.50 (paragraph on soundness of background analysis, page 9). The appraisal document has a section on Involuntary Resettlement OP/BP 4.12 and concludes that the project complies with its requirements (Project Appraisal Document, 29 April 2004). The completion report rates the outcome Unsatisfactory, bank performance Moderately Unsatisfactory and borrower performance Moderately Satisfactory; the Independent Evaluation Group's review of 22 September 2010 (report no. ICRR13381) also rates the outcome Unsatisfactory. Implementing agencies were the Ahwaz Water and Wastewater Company, the Shiraz Water and Wastewater Company and the National Water and Wastewater Engineering Company.

companies.name: Ahwaz Water and Wastewater Company
companies.role: The city-level water and sewerage utility that carried out the Ahwaz half of the project, under the National Water and Wastewater Engineering Company, which is the holding company for Iran's urban water and wastewater utilities and was the third implementing agency. The utility's technical support unit handled procurement and safeguards. No construction contractor is named in the documents for this pumping station.

ahwaz-jomhori-pumping-station-house-expr.community: The project built water and sewerage networks, treatment plants and pumping stations in Ahwaz and Shiraz. The completion report of 31 March 2010 gives one site where land was taken from people. For pumping station AS23-1 on Jomhori Boulevard in Ahwaz, a plot of 800 square metres, the land 'was a residential house that belonged to two individual owners and agreement with them was reached, a down payment was paid, and the property was expropriated'. The report then says: 'Since the deal involved resettlement of at least eight individuals, an abbreviated Resettlement Action Plan (RAP) was prepared.' The report does not say whether the balance of the price was paid, where the eight went, or what they received beyond the price of the house. It says Land Acquisition Plans were prepared wherever land was expropriated and Resettlement Action Plans wherever resettlement of people or displacement of livelihoods was involved, and that several resettlement and land acquisition reviews were carried out during implementation. The Independent Evaluation Group's review of 22 September 2010 says that, according to the completion report, there was adequate compliance with social safeguards policies and procedures in both cities. The appraisal document of 29 April 2004 had said the opposite of what the completion report later recorded at this site: 'In no case are residences or current economic activities or livelihoods affected.' That document also describes, at appraisal, the expropriation in Ahwaz of an unused agricultural plot of 67 hectares from 13 owners, with compensation then being negotiated, and two small undeveloped urban plots for pumping stations taken from private owners. No outcome document found says what happened to those 13 owners. The completion report also records that land acquisition issues caused long delays to the works.
ahwaz-jomhori-pumping-station-house-expr.displaced_label: at least 8 individuals, the figure in the completion report's safeguards section for the house expropriated at Jomhori Boulevard; the report says 'at least eight individuals', so this is a floor and not an exact count
ahwaz-jomhori-pumping-station-house-expr.displaced_note: ICIJ gives 8 for this project, which is its count of project-affected people and not a count of people moved. The figure in the field above is not ICIJ's: it is the completion report's own statement, in its safeguards section, that the expropriation of the house for pumping station AS23-1 'involved resettlement of at least eight individuals'. No other count of people moved appears anywhere in the project's documents.
ahwaz-jomhori-pumping-station-house-expr.outcome: The loan closed on 30 September 2009 with the project unfinished. The completion report says critical components, including treatment plants, pumping stations and pipes, were incomplete or under construction and not fully operational, that unaccounted-for water deteriorated in Ahwaz, and that the financial position of both water companies worsened. It says lack of completion 'will disproportionately affect the poorer segments of the society' because most of the remaining components sit in poor neighbourhoods, and in the same list adds that the proportion of completed works is also higher in poorer neighbourhoods, given the project's focus on the poor. The Independent Evaluation Group's review states the same point in the past tense, that lack of completion 'has disproportionately affected the poorer segments of society'. No later document was found on the house at Jomhori Boulevard or on the eight people.

ahwaz-jomhori-pumping-station-house-expr.confidence_note: The whole of the harm rests on two sentences in the lender's own completion report, backed by the lender's own evaluation review of that report. No independent press report, court record or audit about this expropriation was found; searches in Persian for the pumping station and the boulevard returned nothing on it. The count of eight is the report's floor, 'at least eight individuals', and the report gives no names, no ages and no destination. What the report does say plainly is that a house belonging to two owners was expropriated, that a down payment was paid, and that an abbreviated resettlement plan was prepared because of it. The appraisal document's claim four years earlier that no residence was affected is left unreconciled, as the documents do not explain it.

sources_add.title: Sri Lanka - Metro Colombo Urban Development Project (P122735): Implementation Completion and Results Report
Rehabilitation of St. Sebastian South Canal: Resettlement Action Plan, Project Management Unit, Metro Colombo Urban Development Project (SFG1314)
NHSL flooding: Officials blame 8 houses blocking new drain (The Morning, Methmalie Dissanayake)

fields_add.community: The Bank's completion report for the project (P122735), published on 14 December 2022, puts the total at 652 households affected by the project, through acquisition of private land, recovery of state land occupied by squatter households and the relocation of project-affected households, 'largely the non-titleholder squatter families living along canal banks'. It gives no count of households actually relocated. For St. Sebastian South Canal, the project's Resettlement Action Plan of 8 August 2013, updated August 2014, counts 91 squatter households and says it 'is a regulatory requirement that these 91 households are relocated'; it sets a target of resettling them in individual flats in the condominium at 66 Watte by September 2014, with a transport allowance of LKR 5,000 each, and says the 91 households had expressed willingness to relocate. That figure is a plan, not an outcome, and no Bank document found counts how many actually moved. The completion report names two resettlement sites in use, Methsanda Sevana and Siyasetha Sevana, where women hold four of five and four of six of the building management positions, and records vulnerability allowances of LKR 12.3 million paid to 56 female-headed households living around the drainage works. It also records a second site where people were required to leave their homes. At Norris Canal, completing the works required the relocation of 24 households in a building belonging to the Colombo Municipal Council, which was 'structurally too weak to withstand the deep excavation works, and thus complete demolition was required'. The report describes those 24 as 16 tenants and 8 legal owners holding freehold title under a council deed, then says eight tenants were in the process of relocating because the Supreme Court had decided they should vacate the building, and that the council's acquisition of the properties of 'the four legal owners' under the Land Acquisition Act was in its early stages. The report does not explain the gap between the eight legal owners and the four. At project closure this sub-project was unfinished, with 126 metres of the 675-metre Norris Canal diversion not built, and the report says the project had followed the resettlement process in the plan and that there was no safeguards non-compliance. The project's grievance mechanism recorded 407 grievances in the Bank's text and 423 in the borrower's own section of the same report; 377 were resolved, and the report says the rest were largely about compensation for construction-related damage and would be settled by the contractors through their insurers.
fields_add.outcome: The project closed on 31 December 2021 and the Bank's completion report, dated 14 December 2022, rates the outcome Moderately Satisfactory, bank performance Moderately Satisfactory and monitoring and evaluation Modest, on a loan of which US$199.06 million of the original US$213 million was disbursed. The Norris Canal eviction was still unresolved five years after closure. On 10 November 2026 officials told the Colombo District Coordination Committee that a new drainage route built along Arnold Ratnayake Mawatha towards Beira Lake had 'stalled 100 to 150 metres short of completion because eight structures occupied the stretch', after flash floods on 6 November flooded the ground floors of the National Hospital of Sri Lanka. The residents had been offered alternative housing valued at Rs 5 million and then at about Rs 11 million, and refused both. An official said: 'Since these residents refuse to vacate even after being allocated housing options, we will proceed under the said Act,' meaning the Land Acquisition Act, and Prime Minister Harini Amarasuriya replied: 'Let us proceed accordingly under the Act.' She called for a task force of the Colombo Municipal Council, the District Secretariat, the Urban Development Authority, the police and the armed forces, and a joint meeting on 13 November to make binding decisions on removing unauthorised construction blocking drains.
fields_add.confidence_note: Added in round 32: the Bank's completion report of 14 December 2022 is now the source for the project-wide total of 652 affected households and for the 24 households at Norris Canal; The Morning's report of 11 November 2026 independently records the same eight households still in place, the housing offers they refused and the government's decision to use the Land Acquisition Act, though that report does not mention the World Bank and the tie between those works and the loan comes from the Bank's completion report, which names the same canal and the same unfinished stretch. The two accounts of the unfinished length differ and are left as each gives them: 126 metres of 675 in the completion report, 100 to 150 metres in the newspaper. No count of households actually relocated appears in any Bank document for this project.

morocco-ain-beni-mathar-solar-land.drop_reason: 203 hectares were taken for the Ain Beni Mathar solar and gas plant and the outcome documents record no loss to anyone. The completion report of 25 June 2013 confirms the taking in the past tense in its own annex: '203 hectares of land were acquired by ONEE for the construction and operation of the plant', 160 ha for the plant including 88 ha for the solar field, 6 ha for boreholes, 31 ha for the gas spur and 6 ha for the access road. Those four figures are the ones the brief flagged as appearing in both the appraisal document and the completion report; the verbs differ as the brief said they would, 'will be acquired' in the appraisal and 'were acquired' in the completion report's annex, so the figures are outcomes and not a reprint. The harm is what is missing. The resettlement plan of 1 June 2006 counts the people: 48 persons and bodies affected by the land acquisition, 6 owners at the plant site and 42 persons and bodies for the gas spur, and says 'Aucun deplacement de population n'a ete fait' - no population displacement was carried out - because the parcels were small, unoccupied and not the owners' only source of income. It adds that the individuals farming parcels on the plant site had been compensated at prices set by the administrative valuation commission, and that no monitoring after compensation was planned because no displacement had occurred. On the safeguards side the completion report says: 'Regarding social issues, all measures put forward by ONEE to be in compliance with Bank's policies, e.g. compensation to landowners for loss of agricultural productivity, were considered satisfactory and no particular issues arose.' The evaluation review of 27 June 2014 repeats that, attributing it to the completion report. The one thread worth naming is the collective land: ONEE bought the 160-hectare plant site in June 2005 from the Ministry of the Interior in its capacity as trustee of collective lands, for 7,998,750 dirhams, so the price went to the state and not to the collective's members. The completion report records what became of that money and frames it as a benefit: community projects for one hundred neighbouring families, latrines in three schools and reinforcement of an irrigation system, 'financed with the funds corresponding to the expropriation of collective land for the project', and it lists the same projects again as benefits for women. No document found records any rights-holder of the collective land complaining or going unpaid, and two searches in French for a dispute over the Ain Beni Mathar collective land returned nothing. Neither limb is met: no count of anyone relocated, and no specific loss to identifiable people.

tunisia-fathallah-pesticide-store-occupa.drop_reason: ICIJ's row for Tunisia is a temporary resettlement of eight people that the outcome documents say was carried out and paid for. The abbreviated resettlement plan of 12 May 2011, written for the Fathallah pesticide store in the Jbel Jloud district of Tunis, is the source of ICIJ's figure of 8: the store was occupied by a second-hand clothes sorting shop, and 'Sept ouvriers en plus de l'occupant lui meme seront directement affectes par le projet' - seven workers plus the occupant himself. The loss it identifies is a shortfall in earnings while work on the site suspended the business, with a right to compensation for the period of the works, and a budget of 7,925 Tunisian dinars of which 2,125 dinars was for the compensation of the occupant and his workers. All of it is in the future tense, so it is a plan. The outcome document settles it. The completion report of 28 June 2013 says involuntary resettlement was added to Tunisia's triggered policies in June 2011 at the Level 1 restructuring, that the policy was triggered for the Fathallah store 'that was being used for business purposes by occupants', and that 'Despite smaller incidents and a difficult political environment resulting from the aftermath of the Tunisian revolution, the comprehensive resettlement action plan was implemented and completed to a highly satisfactory extent in June 2012.' In its lessons the same report says the project 'compensated affected individuals financially for their loss in income during their temporary resettlement, and allowed for improved standards of living following the successful disposal of obsolete pesticides at the site.' The report's indicator table records that no accidents were reported, and the Tunisia section says disposal operations were completed without reported incidents or accidents to personnel or damage to the environment. So there is no permanent relocation to count and no uncompensated loss. Two cautions for the record. The resettlement was temporary throughout, which the plan and the report both say; and the 'smaller incidents' the report mentions are not described anywhere in it, so what they were is unknown. This project is filed under two numbers, P103189 and P075776, and the Tunisia documents sit under the second; the row also appears in the west and central Africa batch of this round under ICIJ's separate Mali row, with an estimate of 170, which is a different country and a different set of sites.

afghanistan-justice-service-delivery-lan.drop_reason: The outcome document says no land was taken and nobody moved. The completion report of 28 June 2018 for the Justice Service Delivery Project, the operation ICIJ lists as the second judicial reform project, records construction and rehabilitation of justice buildings in Kabul, Herat, Logar and Bamyan, says OP/BP 4.12 was triggered and a Resettlement Policy Framework was prepared and disclosed in April 2012, and then states: 'However, land acquisition or relocation did not occur as all construction work was carried out on available government land. Overall, no complaint and non-compliance cases were recorded during implementation of the safeguards' instruments under the parent Project.' The only resettlement document harvested, an abbreviated resettlement plan of 18 May 2012, is a three-page statement of principles and process with no site, no census and no figures, and the brief's single candidate sentence from it is the policy recital on replacement cost that fires in every such framework. The evaluation review of 30 September 2018 repeats the completion report's statement and adds that 'The project team later confirmed that there was full compliance, to the best of its knowledge, with safeguard policies' - a staff statement and not a document, and not relied on here. ICIJ's row carries no displacement estimate at all. Neither limb is met.

bangladesh-psdsp-economic-zone-roads.drop_reason: Two resettlement plans under this credit counted 24 households to be displaced, and the outcome documents say the project's resettlement money was never spent. Taking the plans first: the abbreviated resettlement plan for Mirsharai Economic Zone Phase 2, dated August 2016, says the 2,100-acre zone site itself would cause no adverse social impact, but that 'widening of the existing access road into two lanes will displace a total of 14 non-titled households who have been living by the road in public lands, and 5 mosques that have also been built on public lands'. The abbreviated resettlement plan for Mongla Economic Zone, dated April 2015, counts 10 project-affected households: eight leaseholders with small business or dwelling units on the side of the zone's approach road, and two farmers each losing 0.0830 acre for a pumping station at Maniknagar. Both are future tense and both are plans. The completion report of 22 December 2021 is the outcome document and it says the resettlement never happened: Component 2 'also provided resettlement compensation for households affected during the development, but this was ultimately not needed', and the cost table under the additional financing shows the resettlement line at US$0.9 million allocated and US$0.0 million actual, reallocated to other activities because 'the resettlement budget was not needed'. The report says site-specific screenings, resettlement action plans, small ethnic communities plans and gender action plans were prepared and adhered to, that three safeguard policies were triggered - OP/BP 4.01, OP/BP 4.10 and OP/BP 4.12 - and that the project was Category A. Neither the completion report nor the evaluation review of 25 June 2022 mentions Mongla at all, and neither mentions any household displaced. The evaluation review adds that the report carried no overall rating of achieved safeguards compliance and no reporting per policy, and that the last implementation status report rated safeguards compliance Moderately Satisfactory. The gap between the 14 households in the 2016 plan and the unspent resettlement budget in the 2021 report is left unreconciled here, because no document found says what became of them. One outside source bears on it and is the reason this is a drop rather than an unresolved row: the Financial Express of Dhaka reported on 1 March 2019 that the 10-kilometre approach road from Abu Torab on the Chattogram-Dhaka highway to the Mirsharai zone was being built by the Roads and Highways Department at a cost of Tk 1.41 billion, at the request of the economic zones authority, with 46 acres of land for the new section handed over to project officials; it names no World Bank financing and mentions no households or resettlement on the route. On that record the road widening was not paid for by this credit, which is the first of the three tests. No limb (a) count and no limb (b) harm to identifiable people appears in any outcome document.
